newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Pentagon studies Gulf illness report-Cohen.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon studies Gulf illness report-Cohen.

text.p: Responding to a critical congressional report on Gulf War illnesses, U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen promised on Monday to pursue all possible links between biological weapons and complaints by thousands of American veterans of the Gulf War.

"We think that we are making a very strong, good-faith effort to get to the bottom of it," Cohen said at a news conference on a visit to Kuwait. "That is exactly why we have the investigation under way."
He said he had also been critical of previous Pentagon investigation efforts and they had been augmented to include 85 studies in areas including possible biological agents.

Cohen spoke after the New York Times reported that the U.S. General Accounting Office (GAO), the investigating arm of Congress, would issue a report soon criticising the Pentagon and a White House panel for discounting any link between biological agents and troop complaints.

The Defence Department has investigated complaints by more than 60,000 veterans but has found no links to chemical or biological weapons and has said there was no evidence that such arms were used by Iraqi forces during the 1991 war.

"I think we need more evidence, obviously, and we will look very closely at the GAO report," Cohen said, adding that the Pentagon was overseeing broad internal and private studies and would continue its efforts to check every possible source of the complaints, which range from loss of memory to joint aches and headaches.

Cohen told reporters he had not read the report, a draft of which was obtained by the Times, but cautioned that it apparently did not establish a definite link between the veterans' complaints and a possible release of biological agents.
"I don't believe that the reports established that there was a linkage, simply that there was a premature judgment that there was no linkage," the secretary said.
"I have criticised the Defence Department's handling of the investigation myself on several occasions," he told reporters.
"I think that the work that was done previously was not adequate, has a lack of information, maintenance of records, loss of records."
The Times said the report had also found that there was "substantial evidence" linking nerve gas and other chemical weapons to the sorts of health problems seen among the veterans.

The newspaper said the report cautioned that the Defence Department should not rule out the possibility that Iraqi biological weapons, especially a group of potent liver carginogens, might be responsible for some of the ailments.

The Pentagon and a White House panel -- the Presidential Advisory Committee on Gulf War Veterans' Illnesses -- had both concluded that Iraqi chemical and biological weapons were probably not responsible for the veterans' health problems.
Both the Pentagon and the White House committee suggested that the physical after-effects of wartime stress were a more likely cause of most of the ailments.
